title: Ethical Considerations Section
content:
Ethical Considerations Section# An Ethical Considerations section is a specific section in a research paper to describe how the authors considered and addressed the ethical implications of their work. Its purpose is to make potential risks, harms, and broader societal impacts transparent to reviewers and readers, including future researchers.
A starting point suggested by USENIX and the Menlo Report is the Stakeholder-Based Ethics Analysis, including stakeholders and external systems involved in the research and considering their potential for harm (e.g., privacy risks) and benefit. It also explains how these risks were mitigated. Authors may also describe any approvals obtained (e.g., from an ethics board), as well as limitations of their approach and remaining concerns.
Importantly, this section should go beyond formal compliance. Even when no ethics approval is required, researchers are expected to reflect on the consequences of their methods and findings, and to justify why the work is ethically acceptable. Often a good ethics considerations section can already clarify questions that reviewers would have asked anyway.
Stakeholder-Based Ethics Analysis# A stakeholder-based ethics analysis is a structured evaluation of how a research project and its publication may affect all relevant stakeholders such as participants, researchers, companies, and society both now and in the future. It identifies potential benefits and harms, explains mitigations, and justifies whether to proceed using ethical principles.
The following explanation is taken from USENIX Security 2026:
Stakeholders# You are expected to consider all possible stakeholders (people, including the research team and society at large, and entities including companies) that may be impacted by your research. You are expected to detail how each stakeholder may have been impacted by the research procedures you undertook and how those stakeholders may be impacted by the publication of your research now and in the future.
Impacts# Ethical principles: You are expected to articulate the ethical principles you considered. A starting point is considering the principles in The Menlo Report in the context of each identified stakeholder: “Beneficence”, “Respect for Persons”, “Justice”, and “Respect for Law and Public Interest”. Harms: There are at least two broad categories of potentially negative outcomes from the research and publication process: tangible harms (e.g., financial loss or exposure to psychologically disturbing content) and violations of human rights even if there are no directly tangible harms (e.g., the violation of a participants’ right to informed consent or the violation of users’ right to privacy via the study of data that users expect and desire to be private). Mitigations# You are expected to detail both mitigated and unmitigated (potential) harms of your work. You are expected to detail the steps taken to mitigate harms.
Decision# You are expected to articulate why the decision to proceed with the research and the decision to publish the research was reached, respectively. One approach to reaching such a decision is to weigh ethical harms against ethical benefits; see the “Beneficence” principle in The Menlo Report and the 2023 USENIX Security paper, “Ethical Frameworks and Computer Security Trolley Problems.” An alternative or additional approach is to focus on avoiding the violation of individuals’ rights; see the “Respect for Persons” principle in The Menlo Report and the discussion of deontological ethics in the above-cited 2023 USENIX Security paper.
In some cases, the use of different principles in reaching an ethics decision will lead to the same conclusion for what is “right”, e.g., the “Beneficence” and “Respect for Persons” analyses would agree. In other cases, the analyses may lead to different conclusions. If multiple analyses lead to the same conclusions, then documenting all those analyses will provide greater confidence in the ethics of the research. If different analyses lead to different conclusions on the ethics of the research, then the authors should clearly articulate how and why they chose the path they did, even if some principles would have led to a different decision. In some cases, researchers may need to make assumptions about the likelihood of different outcomes or the likely impacts of different decisions; in such cases, the authors are encouraged to articulate and justify all assumptions they make. When considering ethics, researchers and reviewers must acknowledge that, sometimes, the most ethical path is not to do the research or not to publish the research after it is complete. Why do I need it in my paper?# The PC Chairs of USENIX Security ‘26 wrote a post on why they believe all papers should have an ethical considerations section.
Examples# The following table lists a selection of papers we recommend as starting points for examples of well-developed ethics consideration sections.
Crypto:
Li et al. Shred-to-Shine Metamorphosis of (Distributed) Polynomial Commitments. IACR. 2025 Machine Learning:
Gong et al. From Easy to Hard++: Promoting Differentially Private Image Synthesis Through Spatial-Frequency Curriculum. USENIX. 2026 Network and Web:
Chehade et al. 403 Forbidden? Ethically Evaluating Broken Access Control in the Wild. SP. 2025 Pan et al. TORCHLIGHT: Shedding LIGHT on Real-World Attacks on Cloudless IoT Devices Concealed within the Tor Network. USENIX Security. 2025 Heimbach et al. Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue. USENIX Security. 2025 Mustafa et al. LEAKYLINKS: Measuring the Security and Privacy Risks of URL Scanning Services. SP. 2026 Software Security:

title: Ethics Board
content:
Ethics Board# Universities and research institutes worldwide often maintain ethics boards (in the US known as institutional review boards) that review research projects to ensure they meet ethical standards. Researchers may need to obtain approval from such a board before starting their work, particularly when human participants are involved. The following sections outline how these boards operate and highlight country-specific differences.
The process for these boards often starts with a checklist to fill about the current project plus a project proposal. Then a board member reviews the proposal. They then give feedback, request further information or changes to the project.
General problems exist with these boards such as they are often only responsible for human factors research. As they are traditionally designed for human factors research, they also often miss the technical expertise to assess security and privacy projects. This leads to the result that projects might be approved that later by a more technical aware REC are questioned. This is why you should not only trust on the ethics board approval but consider about the ethics of your work beyond the institutional compliance.
General Process# While procedures differ across institutions, the review process usually follows a similar pattern. Researchers begin by submitting a proposal that describes the project’s goals, funding sources, methodology, and potential risks. This submission is often combined with a checklist addressing ethical concerns.
After submission, one or more board members review the proposal. Based on this evaluation, they may approve the project directly, request revisions, or ask for additional clarification. In some cases, approval is conditional on specific changes being implemented. For longer or updated projects, follow-up requests may also be required.
Limitations# Ethics boards are an important safeguard, but they are not a complete solution. Many of these boards were originally designed for biomedical or psychological research (following World War II) and therefore focus primarily on risks to human participants. As a result, they may be less well equipped to assess projects in technical fields such as computer security and privacy.
A common issue is the lack of specialized technical expertise needed to evaluate modern research practices, such as large-scale data collection, analysis of live systems, or vulnerability analysis. This can lead to situations where a project is formally approved but later questioned by more technically informed reviewers or research ethics communities.
Another limitation lies in the underlying goals of different types of review boards. In the United States, Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) often operate with a strong emphasis on regulatory and legal compliance, as well as protecting the institution from liability, an aspect already reflected in the term institutional. In contrast, Ethics Review Boards (ERBs), as commonly referred to in other countries, tend to frame their role more explicitly around ethical reflection and the broader societal implications of research. While this distinction is not absolute, it can influence how reviews are conducted and what aspects receive the most attention.
Additionally, standards and expectations can vary significantly between institutions, leading to inconsistencies in how similar projects are evaluated. For these reasons, ethics approval should not be seen as a definitive judgment. Instead, it should be understood as one component of a broader, ongoing responsibility to reflect on the ethical implications of one’s work.
United States# In the United States, research involving human subjects is regulated under the Common Rule. Approval by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) is mandatory for federally funded research and is typically required by universities and research institutions more broadly.
IRBs are responsible for evaluating potential risks to participants, ensuring that informed consent procedures are appropriate, and safeguarding privacy and confidentiality. Even in computer science, IRB approval may be necessary when research involves user data, experiments with participants, or interactions with online communities.
A list of officially registered IRBs can be found here: https://ohrp.cit.nih.gov/search/irbsearch.aspx
Germany# In Germany, ethics review structures are less standardized. Ethics boards are often referred to as Ethics Review Boards (ERBs) or Ethics Committees, but their structure and availability differ between institutions.
Many established ethics committees are associated with medical faculties and are primarily designed for clinical or human-subject research. As a consequence, researchers in computer science and related technical fields may find that no dedicated review process exists for their work, or that existing boards are not well suited to evaluating it.
This decentralized system can create uncertainty about whether approval is required and how to obtain it. In practice, researchers often need to clarify expectations within their institution or seek alternative forms of guidance when formal review is unavailable.
Practical Advice# It is advisable to clarify early on whether ethics approval is required for a given project and to account for the time such a process may take. When working on projects that involve technical or non-traditional risks, it can be helpful to communicate these clearly and proactively to the reviewing board.
Even when formal approval is not required, documenting ethical considerations and decisions remains important. Seeking feedback from peers or external experts can also provide valuable perspectives, especially in areas where institutional review may lack the necessary expertise.
Ultimately, ethics boards should be seen as a baseline mechanism. Responsible research requires continuous and independent ethical reflection beyond formal approval processes.

title: Ethics Procedure
content:
Ethics Procedure# This section outlines the key ethics-related procedural steps that a research project typically goes through before being approved at a conference.
1. Study Idea# First of all, a good study requires a good idea. Already at this stage, researchers should reflect on the potential ethical implication of their work and their methods, including possible harm and benefits for any stakeholders involved (e.g., users, research team members, etc.), and whether any risks for harm can be minimized through methodological changes or safeguards.
2. IRB / Ethics Board Assessment (Optional)# Depending on the institute, jurisdiction, and research idea, consultation with an Ethics Board or Institutional Review Board (IRB) may also be required.
Certain types of studies, especially those involving human participants, require formal approval by an IRB or an equivalent ethics board. In the United States, IRB review is generally mandatory for human-subjects research, whereas requirements may differ across countries and institutions; researchers should therefore consult local policies to ensure compliance.
Ethics boards typically request a detailed protocol describing the study goals, data collection procedures, participant recruitment (if applicable), potential risks and benefits, consent mechanisms, and planned data protection measures. The goal of this process is to ensure that the study adheres to fundamental ethical principles1 such as respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, and that any risks are justified and appropriately mitigated.
However, due to factors such as limited domain expertise, these boards are often not sufficiently equipped to reliably assess the ethical implications of S&P research. They deal as a first guideline but researchers must reason about the ethics of their work beyond ensuring institutional compliance.
3. Study Execution# Once the study has been approved (if required), the research can be conducted. This phase includes implementing methodology, collecting and processing data, evaluating results, and writing the findings down to a paper.
Throughout execution, researchers should keep an eye out for unanticipated risks or ethical concerns and adjust procedures when necessary to prevent harm. For transparency, any such changes should be documented in the paper (e.g., in the ethical considerations section) so that future researchers can learn from. In some cases, also the ethics boards wants to get informed about any changes!
4. Paper Submission# After completing the study and the paper is submitted to a conference or journal. Besides the typical sections of study such as motivation, background, methodology, limitations, results, and discussion, papers today should also contain a section about ethical considerations. Many venues require specific policies and offer an extra page outside of the page limit for such considerations (see the Conference Guidelines).
5. Peer Review Process# The program committee (PC) evaluates the submission with respect to technical soundness, novelty, and relevance. Increasingly, however, peer review also includes scrutiny of ethical aspects such as the potential for harm of a chosen methodology, compliance with applicable policies (e.g., IRB approval), downstream implications of the publication and whether the researchers followed ethical community norms(e.g., coordinated vulnerability disclosure). In case, reviewers have uncertainties about the ethical acceptability of the submission, they may flag the paper for additional oversight by a conference-internal Research Ethics Committee (REC) or other decision-makers (see the Conference Guidelines).
6. Ethics Revision (Only if flagged for ethics)# If reviewers identify potential ethical concerns, the paper may be escalated to a specialized Research Ethics Committee (REC). This committee evaluates the identified risks in more depth and may consider issues such as missing CVD, lack of informed consent, disproportionate impacts on vulnerable groups, or dual-use concerns.
Based on this assessment, the REC may follow up with the authors to request clarifications, additional context, or revisions to address the identified concerns. In many cases, ethical concerns can be resolved through revisions; however the REC may also recommend rejection if risks or harm was not properly addressed. The final publication decision ultimately rests with the program chairs.
7. Publication# If accepted, the work is published and becomes part of the scientific record 🎉🎉🎉
The publication of research and its results can generate substantial benefits for the research community, as well as for society, for example by improving transparency about specific topics, informing policy and decision makers, or providing tips for more secure and privacy-friendly systems. But publications may also introduce downstream risks such as misuse or unintended harm. As mentioned earlier, this should already be considered in the beginning.
References# Bailey et al. The Menlo Report. SP. 2012 ↩︎

title: IRB Disclosure
content:
IRB Disclosure# Some conferences require authors to get an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval for certain types of projects and mention the assessment in the paper. Requiring ethics approval in the form of an IRB review can be challenging in practice, as not all institutions provide access to such boards or comparable ethics review structures (see Ethics Board).
For this reason, conferences and venues should be cautious about making IRB approval a strict submission requirement 1. A mandatory requirement could unintentionally disadvantage researchers who do not have access to such institutional processes. At the same time, obtaining ethics approval, where available, is strongly encouraged and may already be required by the researcher’s home institution.
However, IRB approval should not be interpreted as a guarantee that a project is ethically sound. As discussed in the context of ethics boards, IRBs often emphasize regulatory compliance and institutional risk management, and they may lack the technical expertise needed to fully assess complex security or privacy research. As a result, important ethical concerns may be overlooked, especially those arising from large-scale measurements, system interactions, or offensive research methodologies.
Ramulu et al. Ethics in Security Research: A Data-Driven Assessment of the Past, the Present, and the Possible Future. CCS 2025. ↩︎

title: Public Statement
content:
Public Statement# Overview# In some cases, PC chairs decide to accept and publish a paper despite ethical concerns raised during the review process. This creates a dilemma: on the one hand, publishing such a paper may appear to reward ethically questionable research; on the other hand, rejecting it does not necessarily prevent it being published at another conference, as the authors may submit it elsewhere, potentially to a venue with less rigorous ethical scrutiny or after modifying the presentation to obscure controversial aspects.
As a compromise, PC chairs may choose to publish the paper with a public statement. This statement is typically included on the first page of the paper or as an accompanying document. It outlines the ethical concerns identified during review, discusses their implications, and explains the reasoning behind the decision to proceed with publication.
The rationale behind this approach is that publishing the work alongside a transparent and critical assessment is preferable to having it appear elsewhere without any contextualization. A public statement can help inform readers and the community, encourage critical engagement, and signal that the work was not uncontroversial within the community.
However, such a statement should not be interpreted as encouraging the methodology or setting a precedent for future acceptance. Rather, it serves as a warning and highlights that the approach may be considered problematic in the future.
Open Questions# The use of public statements remains a topic of ongoing debate within the S&P research community. Critics argue that publication, regardless of a public statement, still provides a signal that such work is acceptable to do as long as the research is interesting enough. Supporters, in contrast, view statements as a way to prevent uncommented publication somewhere else, increase transparency and foster discussion about ethical boundaries.
As a result, there is no clear consensus on whether this practice is desirable. It is still open for discussion.
Examples# Solomos et al. Tales of Favicons and Caches: Persistent Tracking in Modern Browsers. NDSS. 2021. Kircher et al. Dancer in the Dark: Synthesizing and Evaluating Polyglots for Blind Cross-Site Scripting. USENIX Security. 2024. Burnett et al. Encore: Lightweight Measurement of Web Censorship with Cross-Origin Requests. SIGCOMM. 2015. References# Ramulu et al. Ethics in Computer Security Research: A Data-Driven Assessment of the Past, the Present, and the Possible Future. CCS. 2025. Authors. Reflection, Education, Consistency: Towards Best Ethics Practices At Security And Privacy Conferences. CCS. 2026.

title: Research Ethics Committee
content:
Research Ethics Committee (REC)# A Research Ethics Committee is a dedicated body within a conference that conducts ethical reviews of submissions. The committee usually consists of researchers from the community, selected to provide a broad range of perspectives and expertise. REC chairs therefore aim to recruit a diverse group of members to ensure balanced and well-informed assessments.
RECs typically handle papers that have been flagged by reviewers due to potential ethical concerns. When a paper is flagged, it is assigned to one or more REC members, sometimes based on their technical or thematic background. These members review the concerns raised, assess potential risks or harms, and may engage with the authors to clarify uncertainties. This interaction can also help authors improve their paper by making ethical considerations more explicit and transparent.
In addition to providing feedback, RECs can make recommendations to the PC chairs, including suggesting rejection in cases of serious ethical issues. However, final decisions remain with the PC chairs.
Overall, the introduction of RECs brings more structure and consistency to the ethical review process and helps the research community better identify, discuss, and address ethical challenges.

title: Review Form
content:
Review Form# Overview# The review form is the primary way reviewers use to provide feedback about a paper to both the PC and the authors. In addition to general feedback to the paper, most review forms include specific components related to ethical considerations. These elements help structure the discussion and handling of potential ethical issues during the review process.
Ethics Rating# Review forms typically include some sort of rating of the ethical concerns with a submission. This may take the form of a simple binary flag indicating whether concerns exist, or a more fine-grained scale that distinguishes between, for example, no concerns, minor concerns, and major concerns.
Such ratings are particularly useful for RECs, as they provide an initial overview of which papers may require closer inspection. They help prioritize attention and ensure that potentially problematic submissions are not overlooked.
Ethics Concerns# Beyond a rating, review forms usually provide a free-text field where reviewers can describe their ethical concerns in more detail. This written details are essential for enabling both the REC and the authors to understand the concerns, respond to them, and, where possible, improve the work.
Some conferences additionally offer predefined categories of ethical concerns. These can help standardize reporting and assist REC chairs in assigning papers to members with relevant expertise.
Dataset# A dataset of review forms and their ethical components have been collected. The publication of this dataset is currently under discussion.

title: Right to Reject
content:
Right to Reject# Conferences, or more specifically, the PC chairs have the right to reject papers on ethical grounds. This decision is typically made in agreement with reviewers and, where applicable, the Research Ethics Committees.
In practice, this right is used very rarely. Rejecting a paper purely for ethical reasons is generally considered a last resort. As an example, at USENIX Security 2022, the conference rejected only two of the submissions based on ethical concerns1.
In some situations, chairs may choose an alternative approach by accepting the paper with a public statement. that outlines the ethical concerns and justifies the decision to publish despite them.
References# https://docs.google.com/document/d/15x5Qd1UTaoMSRZgRRvurPbgRg4SWWLQKhG41ouYV0TY ↩︎

title: Conference Guidelines
content:
Conference Guidelines# Overview# This section documents the ethics guidelines and practices described by major security and privacy conferences in their Call for Papers (CfPs). It is intended only as a reference and does not guarantee correctness. Authors should always consult the official conference website and the most current policies.
USENIX Security (2026)# USENIX Security requires submissions to include a dedicated section titled Ethical Considerations, which must be placed after the main body of the paper and before the references. This section does not count toward the page limit.
A central expectation is that authors conduct and document a stakeholder-based ethics analysis, explicitly considering who may be affected by the research and how harms were mitigated.
To support ethical evaluation, USENIX has a REC.
IEEE S&P (2026)# IEEE Security & Privacy requires a separate and clearly marked section titled Ethics considerations at the end of every paper. If no ethical considerations apply, authors must explicitly state None in that section. This ethics section does not count toward the page limit.
To support ethical evaluation, S&P has a REC.
IEEE S&P (2027)# IEEE S&P 2027 continues the requirement that authors complete an “Ethics Considerations” field on HotCRP and include an Ethics considerations section in the manuscript at camera-ready (this section does not count toward page limits). If no ethical considerations apply, authors should state None and are encouraged to explain how they reached that conclusion.
To support ethical evaluation, S&P 2027 maintains a REC.
ACM CCS (2026)# ACM CCS requires authors to include an Ethics considerations section for papers that raise ethical concerns that is excluded from the page limit and placed after the primary technical content.
CCS explicitly notes that institutional approval (e.g., IRB/ERB review) is neither strictly necessary nor always sufficient to demonstrate ethical conduct, and that authors are expected to reason about ethical implications beyond formal compliance.
For detailed guidance on community standards, CCS points authors to follow the USENIX Security ’26 ethics policy as a reference baseline.
Instead of a dedicated REC, CCS consults its board of track chairs when ethical concerns arise.
NDSS (2026)# NDSS invites authors to include an optional Ethics Considerations section placed immediately before the references.
Authors should disclose whether IRB (or an equivalent ethics review) was conducted and briefly justify their approach to managing potential risks.
Similar to other major venues, NDSS may escalate submissions with ethics-related concerns to an internal Ethics Review Board (ERB) composed of TPC members.
NDSS (2027)# NDSS invites authors to include an optional Ethics Considerations section placed immediately before the references.
Authors should disclose whether IRB (or an equivalent ethics review) was conducted and briefly justify their approach to managing potential risks.
Similar to other major venues, NDSS may escalate submissions with ethics-related concerns to an internal Ethics Review Board (ERB) composed of TPC members.
Summary Table# Conference Ethics Section Page Limit REC USENIX Security (2026) Required (Ethical Considerations; should contain stakeholder analysis) Excluded from page limit Yes IEEE S&P (2026) Required (Ethics considerations; must state None if not applicable) Excluded from page limit Yes IEEE S&P (2027) Required (Ethics considerations; complete Ethics Considerations field on HotCRP; must state None if not applicable) Excluded from page limit Yes ACM CCS (2026) Required if ethical concerns exist (Ethics considerations) Excluded from page limit No (track chairs handle ethics concerns) NDSS (2026) Optional (Ethics Considerations) Not specified Yes (internal ERB) NDSS (2027) Optional (Ethics Considerations) Not specified Yes (internal ERB)

title: Goals
content:
Goals of Ethics Procedures# Overview# This section outlines the four sets of goals that drive ethics procedures at security and privacy research conferences. These goals were identified through analysis of conference policies and through interviews with senior and junior community members in a recent CCS paper1.
Goal Set 1: Impact on the Outside World# The normative regulation of research activities regarding their impact on the outside world is framed in terms of avoiding harm. Closely related perspectives emphasize the need to prevent malicious uses of research. It can also be understood as protecting people and communities from negative consequences. In addition, considerations extend beyond direct human impact to include potential effects on environmental and computational resources, as well as infrastructures, all of which should be taken into account when assessing possible harm arising from S&P research.
Harm can be understood in two-fold way: (a) a negative consequence directly connected to research activities (e.g., exposing human subjects to excessive stress during an experiment); (b) a negative consequence resulting from the publication of research results (e.g., a study disclosing an unknown vulnerability).
Goal Set 2: Impact on the S&P Community# The impact of ethics procedures on the S&P research community is commonly framed as fostering greater ethical awareness, encouraging researchers to reflect on the ethical dimensions of their work, and promoting education on responsible research practices. In this sense, such procedures can be understood as a pedagogical tool that supports learning how to conduct research in more ethically responsible ways. Beyond individual learning, they also contribute to the development of shared community norms and expectations around ethical conduct. This process of community shaping is reinforced by conferences, which assert and enforce these norms through their authority to reject submissions on ethical grounds. These objectives are reflected, for example, in initiatives such as mandatory ethics sections at USENIX Security 2025 and the expansion of ethics-related requirements in conference calls for papers.
Goal Set 3: Influencing Behavior of Individual Community Members# Goal set 3 is closely related to the preceding set but places greater emphasis on individual members of the research community rather than the community as a whole. In this view, formalized ethics review processes or individual feedback for ethics sections and considerations provide concrete guidance to authors and reviewers and can contribute to improving the overall quality of submitted work. These individual-level objectives are tightly interconnected with community-level goals, as the practices and decisions of authors and reviewers collectively shape broader research norms and standards. At the same time, established community expectations influence individual behavior: failure or refusal to adhere to prevailing ethical standards may result in sanctions, most notably through the rejection of submissions.
Goal Set 4: External Perception# Goal set 4 focuses on how the S&P research community is perceived and evaluated by external stakeholders, including private companies, government agencies, legal institutions, and the broader public. A key element here is to prevent the publication of papers perceived as unethical by the general public. From this perspective, ethics procedures serve to strengthen the reputation and legitimacy of S&P conferences, research institutions, and academic research more broadly. In addition, such measures may function as a form of risk management, including, in some cases, reducing potential legal exposure for conference organizers.
References# Hantke et al. Reflection, Education, Consistency: Towards Best Ethics Practices At Security And Privacy Conferences. CCS 2026. ↩︎

title: Method Specific
content:
Method-Specific Ethics Guidance# This section provides ethics guidance tailored to different research methodologies commonly used in security and privacy research. Each research approach presents unique ethical considerations and challenges.
Overview# Security and privacy research encompasses diverse methodological approaches, each with distinct ethical implications:
Dual-Use Research# Research with legitimate academic or beneficial purposes that could potentially be misused to cause harm. Common in security and cryptographic research where findings could be weaponized.

title: Contributions
content:
How to Contribute# This research ethics wiki is the outcome of and based on a recent research paper1 a community-maintained resource. We welcome contributions from researchers, program committee members, ethics committee members, and anyone interested in advancing research ethics in security and privacy.
To contribute, please open a pull request or start discussing a topic as an issue on GitHub.
For both issues and pull requests, please indicate their purpose by applying the appropriate label:
Correction: Use this label when fixing incorrect or misleading information. Discussion: Use this label for ethics-related topics that you want to discuss with the community. Suggestion: Use this label for general proposals to improve the wiki. Update: Use this label when updating existing information, such as conference policies. Hantke et al. Reflection, Education, Consistency: Towards Best Ethics Practices At Security And Privacy Conferences. CCS 2026. ↩︎

title: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure
content:
Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure# Overview# In security research, vulnerabilities may be discovered in software, hardware, or even the design of some protocol or system. As researchers, we have the responsibility to act in a way to avoid harm affecting users. This is why in most cases when we find a vulnerability, we perform a Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) and help vendors to improve their systems.
If a publication reports vulnerabilities without following a CVD process, this can raise ethical concerns during review. In such cases, authors are typically expected to explain what steps were taken, or why coordinated disclosure was not possible.
Typical Steps# 1. Preparation: Before contacting any party, the vulnerability should be carefully validated. This includes confirming that the issue is real, documenting how it can be reproduced, and assessing its scope and impact. Researchers should also check whether the vulnerability is already known and identify the relevant vendors or stakeholders.
At this stage, it is important to identify appropriate contact channels (e.g., security contacts or disclosure programs) and prepare a clear technical summary. A reasonable disclosure timeline should be considered early on. In practice (1 and 2), timelines often range from 30 to 90 days, depending on severity and complexity.
2. Notification: The responsible parties should be informed without unnecessary delay. The initial report should include enough technical detail for the vendor to understand and reproduce the issue, such as affected systems, versions, and a description of the impact. More information about notifications can be found in academic publications (3 and 4).
Communication should be clear and professional. Researchers typically propose a disclosure timeline and make their intentions transparent. This helps align expectations and reduces the risk of misunderstandings.
3. Response and Coordination: After notification, vendors may ask for clarification or additional information. Researchers are expected to respond in a timely and constructive manner, helping to verify fixes or test patches if needed.
This phase sometimes involves ongoing communication. Keeping records of communication and decisions can also be useful for later documentation.
4. Responsible Publication: Public disclosure usually takes place once a fix is available or the agreed timeline has passed. When publishing, researchers should balance transparency with the risk of misuse and public blaming. This may involve limiting certain technical details or carefully considering whether to release proof-of-concept code.
Example Template:
Subject: Security Vulnerability Report - [Product/System] Dear [Vendor Contact], my name is [Name], and I am a researcher at [Institute]. As part of our recent work on [Topic], we identified a potential security vulnerability affecting [Product/System] version [X.Y.Z]. Based on our analysis, this issue may allow [clear impact e.g., unauthorized access to X / leakage of Y / execution of Z]. To assist your team in reproducing and assessing the issue, we have included detailed steps below: [Vulnerability Description / Reproduction Steps] We are sharing this finding with you under a 90-day responsible disclosure period, aligned with common industry practices. After this period, we may include a description of the issue in a scientific publication. Please let us know if you need any additional information. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Best regards, [Your Name] [Affiliation] [Contact Information]Challenges# While in many cases a CVD is straight forward, there are cases that are challenging and require careful judgment and trade-offs. In such cases, we encourage you to discuss decisions with peers or within your research group. Additional perspectives on these dilemmas can be found in a publication about Computer Security Trolley Problems.
No response in critical cases# A common challenge arises when a vendor does not respond to a vulnerability report. In such situations, researchers need to decide whether and when to proceed with public disclosure.
This decision should take into account the severity of the vulnerability, the likelihood of active exploitation, and the potential impact on users. Publishing may help raise awareness and prompt action, but it can also increase the risk of misuse if no fix is available.
There is no universally correct answer. What matters is that the decision is well thought through, balancing the interests of affected stakeholders, and that the reasoning can be clearly explained, for example, during review or to a REC.
The Dual-Use Dilemma# Vulnerability research is inherently dual-use: the same knowledge that helps defenders can also be used by attackers. This creates a fundamental tension in disclosure decisions.
Making vulnerabilities public can support transparency, improve defenses, and enable independent verification. At the same time, it may lower the barrier for exploitation, especially if mitigations are incomplete or not widely deployed.
Researchers therefore need to consider how much information to disclose and when. This includes decisions about technical detail, proof-of-concept code, and timing. These choices should reflect a balance between advancing knowledge and minimizing harm, while acknowledging that different stakeholders (e.g., users, vendors, and the research community) may be affected differently.
An interesting example for a dial-use consideration is made in a recent publication about the Great Firewall of China5.
References# https://sp2026.ieee-security.org/cfpapers.html#ethical-considerations-for-vulnerability-disclosure ↩︎
https://projectzero.google/vulnerability-disclosure-policy.html ↩︎
Stock et al. Didn’t you hear me? — Towards More Successful Web Vulnerability Notifications. NDSS. 2018. ↩︎
Stock et al. Hey, You Have a Problem: Hey, You Have a Problem: On the Feasibility of Large-Scale Web Vulnerability Notification. USENIX. 2016. ↩︎
Zohaib et al. Exposing and Circumventing SNI-based QUIC Censorship of the Great Firewall of China. USENIX. 2025. ↩︎

title: Datasets
content:
Datasets# Security and privacy research often relies on datasets collected by others. These datasets can be extremely valuable, especially when they provide insight into real-world attacks, user behavior, vulnerabilities, abuse ecosystems, or failures of deployed systems. However, some of these datasets were obtained through questionable, unauthorized, or illegal means like password leakage datasets or exposed server logs. This aspect has led to discussion within the community (see 1 and 2).
Publicly Available Does Not Mean Ethically Public# A common argument is that a dataset is acceptable to use because it is already public. This is not sufficient. Data may be technically accessible while still being private, sensitive, or published against the wishes and expectations of the people affected.
For example, a password dump posted online may be easy to download, but the affected users did not consent to their passwords being exposed or studied. Similarly, leaked emails, private messages, or account records may remain sensitive even if they are circulating publicly. Researchers should therefore distinguish between:
data that was intentionally made public data that was accidentally exposed data that was stolen or leaked The more questionable the origin of the dataset, the stronger the ethical justification and safeguards need to be.
When Use May Be Justifiable# Using a questionable dataset is not automatically unethical, but it requires careful justification. A study may be more acceptable when:
the research question is important and cannot reasonably be answered with safer data the dataset is uniquely valuable for understanding or reducing real-world harm the researchers took careful safeguards to secure the dataset the researchers did not participate in or encourage the original wrongdoing the work does not create new victims or substantially increase risk to existing victims the data is processed in a minimized, secure, and privacy-preserving way raw sensitive data is not redistributed the results are reported at an appropriate level of aggregation legal and institutional review has been considered the paper clearly explains the ethical reasoning Weak justifications include: “others have used it before”, “attackers already have it”, “it was easy to find”, or “it is technically public”. These arguments may be relevant to the risk analysis, but they are not enough on their own.
Questions to Ask Before Using a Dataset# Before using a dataset, researchers should ask:
Origin: How was the dataset obtained? Was it collected with consent, leaked, stolen, scraped, purchased, or exposed by accident? Legality: Could downloading, storing, processing, or sharing the dataset violate laws, contracts, terms of service, or institutional rules? Sensitivity: Does the dataset contain passwords, tokens, private messages, financial data, health data, sexual content, political views, location traces, children’s data, or other sensitive information? Identifiability: Can individuals or organizations be identified directly or through linkage with other data? Necessity: Is this dataset necessary, or could the research question be answered with synthetic data, aggregated data, consented data, public documentation, or a less sensitive source? Benefit: What concrete scientific, security, privacy, or societal benefit does the study provide? Harm: What is the worst plausible harm if the dataset, code, model, or derived results are misused? Safeguards: How will access, storage, processing, deletion, and sharing be controlled? Publication: Could the paper help attackers find, reconstruct, validate, or exploit the data? Safeguards# Appropriate safeguards depend on the dataset and the research question, but may include:
avoiding download of raw illegal data where possible storing data encrypted and access-controlled limiting access to approved project members keeping an access log replacing raw values with hashes if feasible avoiding publication of example records from real people publishing only aggregate statistics using synthetic examples in the paper and artifact not linking to, naming, or making the leaked dataset easier to find deleting the data after the project when retention is no longer justified documenting the data lifecycle in the ethics section What to Report in the Ethics Section# Papers using sensitive, leaked, hacked, or otherwise questionable datasets should include a dedicated ethics discussion. This section should explain:
Dataset origin: What is known about how the dataset was created, leaked, exposed, or obtained? Permission and consent: Was consent or permission obtained? If not, why was this infeasible, and how were affected people’s interests protected? Legal and institutional review: Was an IRB, ethics board, legal office, data protection officer, or equivalent body consulted? If not, why not? Necessity: Why was this dataset needed, and what alternatives were considered? Risks: What harms could arise from possession, analysis, publication, or artifact release? Benefits: What concrete benefits justify the use of the dataset? Safeguards: How was the data stored, minimized, transformed, protected, and eventually deleted? The goal is to show that the researchers understood the origin and sensitivity of the data, considered the people and organizations affected, weighed harms against benefits, and chose safeguards appropriate to the risk.
References# Egelman et al. It’s Not Stealing If You Need It: A Panel on the Ethics of Performing Research Using Public Data of Illicit Origin. Workshop on Ethics in Computer Security Research. 2012. ↩︎
Thomas et al. Ethical Issues in Research Using Datasets of Illicit Origin. IMC. 2017. ↩︎

title: Live Systems
User Studies
content:
User Studies# From S&P: Submissions that describe experiments that could be viewed as involving human subjects, that analyze data derived from human subjects (even anonymized data), or that otherwise may put humans at risk should:
Disclose whether the research received an approval or waiver from each of the authors’ institutional ethics review boards (e.g., IRB) if applicable. Discuss steps taken to ensure that participants and others who might have been affected by an experiment were treated ethically and with respect. If a submission deals with any kind of personal identifiable information (PII) or other kinds of sensitive data, the version of the paper submitted for review must discuss in detail the steps the authors have taken to mitigate harms to the persons identified. If a paper raises significant ethical and/or legal concerns, it will be checked by the REC and it might be rejected based on these concerns. The PC chairs will be happy to consult with authors about how this policy applies to their submissions.
